20th November 2005.

A date permanently engraved in my memory.

The day I entered a gym for the first time.

And 21 years later, I have never looked back.

But there is a story behind that decision.

Before 2005, falling sick was almost an annual ritual for me.

Every year, some fever would knock me down for 5–7 days.

Then came October 2005.

In the first half of October, I suffered a viral fever that lasted nearly 7–10 days.

Barely 10–12 days after recovering, I was struck by something far more serious.

Severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria.

Two illnesses. Almost back to back.

I still remember the weakness, the exhaustion, and the frustration of being physically helpless.

After recovering, I made a promise to myself.

Enough. I cannot control every disease, but I can certainly work on the body that has to fight it.

On 20th November 2005, I walked into a gym.

Not to build six-pack abs.

Not to impress anyone.

Not to look muscular.

I went there because I was tired of feeling physically vulnerable.

What followed surprised even me.

Over the next two decades, I can recall hardly 6–7 episodes of mild cold.

No comparable prolonged febrile illness, even during my medical postings through the COVID years.

Was it all because of the gym?

I cannot scientifically claim that.

But regular exercise, better nutrition, improved sleep habits, and a disciplined lifestyle completely transformed my relationship with my body.

That malaria episode lasted days.

The decision it triggered has lasted decades.

Sometimes, the worst days of your life become the foundation of your strongest years.

20th November 2005 wasn’t the day I started bodybuilding.

It was the day I stopped taking my health for granted.

The Striking Devil
.
Striking hammers are prepared for the bodies of sinners.
.
The devil gave Job one stroke, only one stroke. That one stroke was so terrible that it covered all his body with sores and ulcers. That one stroke made Job look so frightful, that his friends did not know him again. That one stroke was so terrible, that for seven days and seven nights his friends did not speak a word, but sat crying, and wondering, and thinking what a terrible stroke the devil can give.
.
Little child, if you go to hell there will be a devil at your side to strike you. He will go on striking you every minute for ever and ever, without ever stopping. The first stroke will make your body as bad as the body of Job, covered from head to foot with sores and ulcers. The second stroke will make your body twice as bad as the body of Job. The third stroke will make your body with three times as bad as the body of Job. The fourth stroke will make your body four times as bad as the body of Job. How then will your body be after the devil has been striking it every moment for a hundred million of years without stopping?
.
But there was one good thing for Job. When the devil had struck Job, his friends came to visit and comfort him, and when they saw him they cried. But when the devil is striking you in hell, there will be no one to come and visit and comfort you, and cry with you. Neither father, nor mother, nor brother, nor sister, nor friend will ever come to cry with you. Lam.i. "Weeping she hath wept in the night, and the tears are on her cheeks, because there is none to comfort her amongst all them that were dear to her." Little child, it is a bad bargain to make with the devil, to commit a mortal sin, and then to be beaten for ever for it.
.
The Mocking Devil
.
Shall they not take up a parable against him, a dark speech concerning him?
.
St. Francis saw that on the other side of the soul there was another devil to mock at and reproach it. Hear what mockeries he said to it. "Remember," he said, "remember where you are and where you will be for ever; how short the sin was, how long the punishment. It is your own fault; when you committed that mortal sin, you knew how you would be punished. What a good bargain you made to take the pains of eternity in exchange for the sin of a day, an hour, a moment. You cry now for your sin, but your crying comes too late. You liked bad company, you will find bad company enough here. Your father was a drunkard, and showed you the way to the public-house; he still is a drunkard, look at him over there drinking red hot fire. You were too idle to go to Mass on Sundays, be as a idle as you like now, for there is no Mass to go to. You disobeyed your father, but you dare not disobey him who is your father in hell; look at him, that great chained monster; disobey him if you dare."
.
St. Francis saw that these mockeries put the soul into such dreadful despair of that it burst out into the most frightful howlings and blasphemies.
.
But it is time for us now to see where the sinner has been put -- his everlasting dwelling-place.

A Bed of Fire
.
The sinner lies chained down on a bed of red-hot blazing fire! When a man, sick of fever, is lying on even a soft bed, it is pleasant sometimes to turn round. If the sick man lies on the same side for a long time, the skin comes off, the flesh gets raw. How will it be when the body has been lying on the same side on the scorching, broiling fire for a hundred millions of years! Now look at that body lying on the bed of fire. All the body is salted with fire. The fire burns through every bone and every muscle. Every nerve is trembling and quivering with the sharp fire. The fire rages inside and the skull, it shoots out through the eyes, it drops out through the ears, it roars in the throat as it roars up a chimney. So will mortal sin be punished. Yet there are people in their senses who commit mortal sin!

“Seven years ago. Liver failure. I heard from someone at your old office.”

I closed my eyes. A man I had once mistaken for escape had become only a shadow. I felt no love. No grief. Only a dull sadness for all the ruin born from hunger and loneliness.

“Did you hate me more after that?” I asked.

Arvind turned his face toward the window. “I hated myself more.”

“Why?”

“Because part of me was relieved.”

The honesty sat between us, ugly and human.

“I understand,” I said.

“Do you?”

“Yes. Because part of me spent years wishing you would shout, hit me, leave me, do anything except be decent in front of the world and dead beside me. Then I hated myself for wishing cruelty from a good man.”

His eyes shone. “I was not good, Naina. I was proud. Wounded. Afraid. I wanted to protect you, but I also wanted you to remember what you had broken.”

“I did.”

“I know.”

“I am sorry.”

“I know.”

“Will you ever forgive me?”

He closed his eyes. “I forgave you many years ago.”

The words stopped my breath.

“Then why...”

“Because forgiveness is not the same as knowing how to return.”

I bent my head and cried into my saree.

After a while, I felt something touch my hair. Light. Trembling. Barely there.

Arvind's fingers.

For the first time in eighteen years, my husband touched me. Not like a lover. Not yet. Like a man opening the door of a house he thought had burned down.

I did not move. I did not breathe.

His hand stayed on my head for three seconds. Then five. Then ten.

When he pulled away, both of us were crying.

---

The treatment was not easy. Hospitals are not places where love becomes pretty. Love there is paperwork, urine bottles, unpaid bills, tablet alarms, arguing with nurses, learning side effects, pretending the blood report is not frightening.

Arvind's body had suffered too long in silence.

There were bad nights. Nights when fever burned him. Nights when he pushed food away. Nights when he whispered, “Let me go,” and I whispered back, “Not until you learn how to be properly stubborn with me again.”

I moved into the hospital chair. Then into our bedroom after he came home.

The first night back, he stood at our bed and looked at the white pillow in the middle. It was old now. Flat. Faithful. Hateful.

He picked it up. His hands shook. “I don't know how to sleep without it.”

I nodded. “Then we won't throw it.”

His face fell.

I took the pillow from him and placed it at the foot of the bed. “Not between us. But not forgotten.”

He looked at me for a long time. Then he lay down on his side. I lay beside him.

There was space between us. A cautious, trembling space. But no wall.

At two in the morning, thunder rolled over Mumbai.

I woke, heart racing. Arvind was awake too.

I whispered, “Arvind...”

For eighteen years, he would have said, “Sleep.”

That night, he turned his head. “Yes?”

The word broke something open inside me.

“Can I hold your hand?”

Fear crossed his face. Then trust. Then fear again. Finally, slowly, he placed his hand palm-up on the sheet.

I put mine over it.

His skin was warm. Thin. Alive.

We lay like that until morning. Not healed. Not young again. Not innocent. But together in the truth.

---

Months passed.

The children noticed before anyone else. Priya saw us sitting closer during tea and burst into tears in the kitchen. Rohan caught Arvind adjusting my shawl and stared like he had witnessed a miracle.

Relatives said retirement had made him soft. Neighbors said illness had made me devoted.

Let them. People always prefer simple stories. They cannot bear the messy ones where sin and sacrifice sleep in the same bed for eighteen years and still wake up breathing.

Common Bacteria Found on Floors:

Staphylococcus species (including Staphylococcus aureus and MRSA): Naturally live on human skin and shed into house dust. Methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) can persist on floors and cause skin or systemic infections.

Escherichia coli (E. coli): Tracked in via shoe soles or pet/human fecal contamination; common on soil floors, public restrooms, and entryways.

Salmonella species: Brought in via shoes, pets, or food debris dropped on the floor, capable of causing severe gastrointestinal illness.

Clostridium difficile (C. diff): Form highly resilient spores that frequently contaminate hospital and residential floors, sometimes surviving in higher concentrations on floors than on bedrails

Enterococcus species (including VRE): Vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus is commonly isolated from floor dust and healthcare surfaces

Campylobacter: Often found in moist environments or areas exposed to pet/poultry waste.

Pseudomonas aeruginosa: An opportunistic pathogen thriving in damp conditions. ( it can let you blind)

Other Common Genera: Micrococcus, Streptococcus, Corynebacterium, Propionibacterium, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Janthinobacterium, and Microbacterium (frequently mapped in indoor microbiome and dust studies.

Common Viruses Found on Floors
Norovirus: The "stomach flu" virus, which can survive on hard surfaces and carpet fibers for days to weeks and become airborne when someone walks across the floor.

Influenza Virus: Can settle on hard, non-porous floor surfaces and remain infectious for up to 24–48 hours.

Rhinovirus: The primary cause of the common cold; studies show rhinovirus can transfer from contaminated floor tiles via direct contact.

Human Papillomavirus (HPV) & Herpes Simplex Traces: Frequently detected via genetic sequencing on public or high-traffic restroom floors.

SARS-CoV-2 RNA: Can occasionally be detected on floor dust and high-traffic surfaces in shared or healthcare environments.

Meningitis: The classic clinical triad of meningitis consists of fever, headache, and nuchal rigidity (neck stiffness), frequently accompanied by altered mental status and photophobia (sensitivity to light) due to inflammation of the protective membranes (meninges) surrounding the brain and spinal cord.
Pneumonia: Primarily presents with cough, fever, shortness of breath, and pleuritic chest pain.
Malaria: Characterized by cyclic fevers, chills, sweats, and rigors, often accompanied by myalgias and fatigue, but does not present with the classic meningeal signs.

A Nonprofit AI Lab Built Headphones With Rat Ears to Play Rats' Ultrasonic Calls

The lab is Basis, a nonprofit applied AI research organization founded in 2022 by Zenna Tavares, Emily Mackevicius, and Eli Bingham. It has offices in New York and Cambridge, Massachusetts, and its stated goal is a universal reasoning engine, built as open-source software, that helps society solve hard problems.

The headphones were part of an exhibit on October 30 at City Creatures, a pest control company's event at Terra Gallery in San Francisco. Basis researchers Ralph Peterson and Nick Jourjine used a pitch-shifting algorithm to lower rats' ultrasonic calls into the range people can hear, keeping each call's original length and timing.

Visitors compared the calls to bird songs and a whining dog, and one described a call as sounding alarmed. Peterson said listeners picked up different emotions in the rats' voices.

The calls come from Basis's urban rat monitoring. Mackevicius leads its Collaborative Intelligent Systems group, which brings together neuroscientists, cognitive scientists, mathematicians, engineers, and behavioral ecologists to study animals in the wild.

The work has been covered by Scientific American, The New Yorker, CBS, WBUR, and Northeastern. The team has also built 3D models of rats moving around dumpsters, which Basis ties to its broader goal of AI systems that can reason about the real world.

Basis has no venture investors. It is a 501(c)(3) public charity, tax-exempt since December 2022, and it takes donations. Its tax filings, as reported by data sites, show about $4.7 million in revenue and $2.9 million in expenses in the latest year, with 92% of spending going to programs. Reported assets are about $4.1 million. Its site doesn't list donors.

The other work is software and verification. On November 10, Basis released Dynestyx, an open-source library for modeling systems that change over time, from epidemics to turbulent flows. It gives researchers one interface for building a model and trying different inference methods.

Basis shows it filtering a 256-by-256 fluid flow from noisy 32-by-32 observations and forecasting a 1978 boarding school flu outbreak. It also says combining standard algorithms in the library led to what it believes is a new best-in-class inference method, with results to come.

In July, Basis used LLMs to verify part of Linux's network stack and patched bugs that had sat in the kernel for years. In April, it had four agents spend 14 days writing 93,000 lines of Lean to build a verified JavaScript-to-WebAssembly compiler. The compiler ran, but the proofs didn't close.

Mackevicius says the exhibit pushed the team to look at its data more slowly, almost at the pace of a rat.

Charcot's Triad — the classic clinical presentation of acute ascending cholangitis (an acute bacterial infection of the biliary tract, most commonly secondary to choledocholithiasis).  
Clinical Breakdown
Fever (with chills/rigors): Reflects bacteremia and systemic inflammatory response caused by bacterial translocation from the infected biliary tree into the bloodstream.  
Right Upper Quadrant (RUQ) Abdominal Pain: Caused by biliary tract obstruction and acute distension/inflammation of the bile ducts.  
Jaundice: Results from impaired biliary drainage and conjugated hyperbilirubinemia due to mechanical obstruction (typically a gallstone in the common bile duct).

I have taken about 900 thousand photos of Texas. There are few that stick with me more than this one, which I post here every Veteran's day.  This is a ceramic photograph that I found on a grave marker in a rural black cemetery near Giddings. The cemetery is fairly remote, such that there's no way I could navigate back to it without the help of a map.  

The inscription on the tombstone reads: 
Pvt. Clinton Francis 
Born March 29, 1893 
Died Nov. 24, 1918 
A Soldier's Death  

I initially thought that Private Francis must have died from wounds he received during World War I, but some of y'all tracked him down via genealogy records and his death certificate reads that he died of tuberculosis. My guess is that perhaps that is actually incorrect and that he died of the Spanish Flu that was raging that year. 

 But look at him looking back at us though the generations! See how handsome he is in his uniform and his gloves and his boots.  

I can't say why this photo sticks with me.  Anybody who knew Private Francis is long gone. He is now just a forgotten man in a lonely cemetery, dust blowing around the corner, smoke slipping through a keyhole, a shaft of sunlight coming through a window in an old room.  

But I have not forgotten you, Private Francis!  Every Veteran's day, I remember. And I raise my glass to you and to the uncountable others and offer only the hope that we not let the memories of your sacrifices be forgotten.  A soldier's death, indeed.

➡️ Avian Flu Outbreak in Illinois Spread from Backyard Poultry to Mammals

— An outbreak of highly pathogenic avian influenza A ➡️ (H5N1) virus that devastated an Illinois backyard flock also ➡️ infected a domestic cat ➡️ and wild rats on the property, according to a case study conducted by diagnostic laboratories in Illinois and Missouri.

Cases and health response

- The findings demonstrate that ➡️ the virus extended beyond the poultry coop to multiple mammalian species present on the farm premises.

- The case originated in March 2025 after a farmer experienced a rapid die-off, losing 100 out of 105 backyard birds.

- Following the flock mortality, ➡️ the farmer transported the remains of five birds along with a rat carcass to the University of Missouri diagnostic facility, where testing confirmed that a chicken sample was positive for avian influenza.

- Four days after the initial poultry testing, the farm’s primary veterinarian submitted the remains of a domestic cat and an additional wild rat to the University of Illinois Veterinary Diagnostic Laboratory.

- A research team led by Dr. Leyi Wang, virology section head at the laboratory and a professor of veterinary clinical medicine, examined the specimens and confirmed that ➡️ both mammals were infected with the same H5N1 subtype found in the poultry flock.

Health investigation

- The investigation, published in the journal Emerging Infectious Diseases, was carried out by researchers at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign Veterinary Diagnostic Laboratory and the University of Missouri Veterinary Medical Diagnostic Laboratory.

- Situated two miles from a reservoir lake, ➡️ the farm occupied a geographic setting conducive to viral transmission from wild waterfowl to domestic poultry.

posts.text:
Based on the 2024 Michigan & Colorado farmworker data and the 2026 WA genomes, two things are almost certainly true at once:

1. Genuine cow-to-human H5N1 IS undercounted.

In 2024 MI/CO serology, ~7% of exposed dairy workers had H5 antibodies—most had mild illness and were never PCR-tested. With 43 WA herds hit in ~4 weeks and real economic/immigration barriers to testing, 3 official cases is almost certainly an undercount.

2. Untested "severe avian flu symptoms" in November are heavily confounded by seasonal viruses.

There is no symptom that separates respiratory H5N1 from seasonal Flu A (H1N1/H3N2), COVID-19, or RSV: fever, cough, and body aches are generic immune responses. In 2024 CO/MI/CA farmworker testing, the vast majority of workers with systemic flu-like symptoms tested negative for H5N1 and positive for ordinary respiratory viruses.

3. Why exposure route matters (Cows vs. Human-to-Human).

• Cow-to-human (milking parlor): Human eye tissue carries "avian-type" (α2,3) receptors, while our upper airway carries "human-type" (α2,6) receptors. Raw-milk splash/aerosols hit the eye—making acute pinkeye (conjunctivitis), often without high fever, the signature B3.13 dairy worker symptom (>90% of US dairy cases).

• Both sequenced WA human H5N1 genomes sit directly inside the WA cattle cluster (2–4 SNPs from cows) with no fixed human-transmission sweep—pointing to independent cow-to-worker exposures, whereas fevers/coughs spreading between coworkers or households in November are more likely seasonal flu or other respiratory illnesses.

Low-barrier, confidential paired testing (both eye + nasal swabs on a multiplex panel) can separates H5 from seasonal Flu A, COVID & RSV.

Choosing a product that matches your specific symptoms makes more sense than treating everything at once. A newly identified SARS-CoV-2 variant, PJ.2.1, is drawing global attention after rapidly spreading across North America, Europe, Asia, and Australia.

Here are the key facts and expert insights on what this means:

🔹 What is it?

PJ.2.1 is a "novel saltation variant" (meaning it carries multiple new spike protein mutations) descended from the JN.1 lineage. It was first detected in Canada in May 2026 and quickly became one of the fastest-growing variants in the US.

🔹 Key Symptoms:

Symptoms mirror a standard cold or flu: fever, severe sore throat, cough, fatigue, headache, and body aches. Testing is recommended if symptoms persist.

🔹 Is it More Dangerous?

According to a study published in the Journal of Infection (Oct 2026), PJ.2.1 binds more efficiently to human cells, allowing it to spread faster. However, there is no evidence that it causes more severe disease, higher hospitalisation rates, or evades antibody protection from updated vaccines.

🔹 Expert Advice:

Health experts emphasize monitoring over panic.

 * Wear masks in crowded, poorly ventilated spaces.

 * Practice regular hand hygiene.

 * High-risk individuals (elderly, immunocompromised, or those with underlying conditions) should consult their doctor regarding updated boosters and take extra precautions.

Couple thoughts:

1) After several people pointed out that Lyman couldn't substitute all-cause mortality for malaria-specific mortality like he had done, he fixed it. His initial estimate for $/lives saved was $19000; revised it’s about $8,200. 

2) I think, though I could be wrong about this, that his calculation to get $8200 still has a problem: he calculates the costs of the distribution based on the whole population but the benefits based on 75% of the population (since he argues the other 25% is already sleeping under nets). But as he himself identifies, the nice thing about an intention-to-treat analysis is that you don't need to do this and shouldn't: you just ask how much to expect mortality to fall in a village after handing out the nets, and the answer is 17%. (You only care about the fact some people are already sleeping under nets if that makes your village unlike the one where the  17% was measured; more on that below.) If he changed this one factor this would make his numbers quite close to GiveWell's.

3) He then applies an adjustment for the long-term: "If bednets reduced short-run all-cause mortality by 18% in the 1990s and maybe reduce it by (who knows?) 14% today, they probably reduce actual child mortality (i.e. across 5 years of early childhood) by 7-11%." 

But GiveWell actually accounts for that even more stringently by just excluding all benefits past the first two years, one of several places where they are intentionally conservative. 

4) He accuses GiveWell of misrepresenting Cochrane's statistics  but they actually just report a bunch of different numbers and I think he mixed them up. He complains "GiveWell cites that review to support a “45% reduction in malaria incidence.” That’s an error, that review did not find a 45% reduction in malaria incidence." But the review absolutely does report almost exactly that: "Insecticide-treated nets also reduce the incidence of uncomplicated episodes of Plasmodium falciparum malaria by almost a half (rate ratio 0.55, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.64; 5 trials, 35,551 participants, high-certainty evidence". Rate ratio 0.55 means a 45% reduction. 

5) He expresses concern that a lot of the Cochrane studies are old and describe a different environment (Africa in the late 1990s/early 2000s). However, GiveWell's most recent grant to nets in the DRC - which I believe that my donations helped to fund - is based on data from a 2023-2024 large scale demographic survey in the DRC, so the nets are being distributed in an environment very close to the one studied. It found about a 14% all-cause mortality reduction in the first year after a distribution, close to the 17% in Cochrane. 

He also expresses concern that Cochrane's mortality estimate here is low-powered but I don't think it is (the analysis says "rate ratio 0.83, 95% CI 0.77 to 0.89; 5 trials, 200,833 participants, high-certainty evidence") so it's between 11% and 23% with a 95% CI!

6) He also raises questions about whether there are more people trying to hand out nets than nets to be handed out. GiveWell looked into that and determined that in the DRC, there was not enough funding to do all the distributions that were indicated, in part because the Global Fund caps how much it'll spend in any one country. 

7) Finally, he argues we should instead - from an altruistic perspective - spend our money however maximizes GDP. But I think there's a serious case that health interventions like combatting malaria are necessary for GDP growth to take off in DRC, just like the American South was kind of a backwater until we eradicated malaria there. Being constantly sick is horrible for productivity. Being only able to hire employees who are constantly sick is horrible for a business environment. GiveWell estimates that a $1,000,000 donation increases adult income for 80,000 children by 0.6%, which means that much of their modelled benefit of malaria nets *is* their GDP effects.

My best guess is that if you were a hard-nosed GDP maxxer you'd invest a lot in reducing the disease burden in poor countries.  Or maybe you'd go all in on making AI happen as fast as possible, something I rarely see EAs criticized for failing to do. I would probably donate more money to making AI go well if I had more of an idea of how to do that and it wouldn't create a bunch of conflicts of interest with my reporting work.

I agree it would be cool if there were an organization focused on effective institutional capacity building in poor countries, but the reason I and man others don't donate to this is not that everyone fails to realize how important institutions are, it's that even though many people have worked very hard on the problem for a long time they do not have a way better than the nets to turn my money into GDP growth in poor countries.

Right now in the Twentynine Palms area and broader San Bernardino County, public health officials are tracking a notable, early surge in influenza (specifically the H1N1 strain) alongside elevated levels of rhinovirus and enterovirus (the primary drivers of the common cold). 
Local health alerts show that viral respiratory season has hit earlier and harder than usual this year. If you or someone you know is battling a severe head cold, it is likely one of the following circulating bugs: 

Influenza (H1N1): San Bernardino County health officials have issued warnings regarding an early, aggressive uptick in H1N1 flu cases. While it often presents with sudden fever, severe body aches, and fatigue, it can also cause intense head congestion and headaches.
Rhinovirus and Enterovirus (RV/EV): These standard "common cold" viruses are currently elevated nationally and regionally. They are the classic culprits behind severe sinus pressure, runny or stuffed nose, sore throat, and a hacking cough. 
COVID-19 and RSV: While CDC data shows COVID-19 activity is generally declining and RSV remains relatively low at the moment, both continue to circulate alongside early flu cases. 

When to Seek Medical Attention

Most viral "head colds" can be managed at home with plenty of rest, fluids, and over-the-counter symptom relievers. However, because the H1N1 flu strain is moving through the community aggressively, you should consult a doctor right away if you experience any of the following warning signs: 
Difficulty breathing or severe shortness of breath
A high fever that doesn't come down with medication
Confusion, dizziness, or severe weakness
Symptoms that initially improve but then return significantly worse
Persistent, severe chest or sinus pain

posts.text:
An ICU doctor with mild COVID could not stand to shower, and when a code blue came she sat down to run the code.

Sonali Mantoo, a critical care physician, says it began like the flu: a low-grade fever, a hacking cough, one urgent care visit. She was fit, did yoga and dance, and expected to bounce back. Then she could not walk 10 or 20 feet without being short of breath.

“I would sit down to run the code, and then I was like, this is not sustainable.”

Her first long COVID specialist told her, “you could very well live like this for the rest of your life.” She was gasping for air, holding a walking stick, and told him, “that’s not a very nice thing to say to somebody who’s struggling.”

Her message: “Long COVID is real. Real.”

Metal fume fever is a short-lived flu-like reaction mainly from inhaling fresh zinc oxide fumes (common when heating or welding galvanized steel). 

Symptoms—fever, chills, muscle/joint aches, headache, metallic taste, fatigue, sometimes cough—usually start 4–12 hours after exposure and resolve on their own in 24–48 hours. 

Treatment is supportive: rest, fluids, and over-the-counter fever/pain relief. No lasting effects in typical cases. Fresh fumes are the trigger; ordinary zinc dust is far less likely to cause it.

posts.text:
Mold can live inside you, in your sinuses, your lungs and your gut, so when you move out of a moldy house, it can come with you.

Say you take the big step and move out, and you still don't get better. Many people don't. There are two explanations, and you may have both. The first is that your body is still overloaded with the toxins it built up. The second is that the mold came with you.

I saw this with a client I'll call John. He'd been ill for over 40 years and had moved house many times without getting better. When we tested his home, one species of Aspergillus, a type of mold, was over 100 times the maximum safe allowed level. He had the house remediated, then moved to a different house he'd made sure had no mold first. He got somewhat better, especially after the move. But his IgE, the antibody involved in allergies, was still above the maximum level, and there were other signs he was still struggling with toxicity. That's when I looked for mold growing in his airways, and it was there: he was diagnosed with a fairly severe aspergillus infection. Once we treated that, along with a thorough protocol to support his liver, he started feeling better and better.

So if you've moved out and you're still not improving, and you have sinus problems, a cough that won't go away, trouble breathing or digestive symptoms, ask a practitioner to look at whether the mold came with you, instead of doing another detox. Those symptoms can all be there without any mold living in you, so it's a suspicion rather than a diagnosis. With your sinuses, it's better to test than to assume, because sinus trouble could just as easily be an allergy or an intolerance.

Saline nasal rinse for congestion: how to do it safely.

WHAT IT IS: A saltwater solution flushed through the nasal passages with a neti pot, squeeze bottle or rinse kit.

WHAT IT DOES: It thins mucus and washes out allergens, dust and irritants. Studies show it can ease congestion and sinus symptoms from colds and allergies.

HOW TO USE:

Use only distilled or sterile water, or tap water that’s been boiled for 1 minute and cooled until lukewarm. Never use plain tap water.
Mix a premixed saline packet with the water, or follow the kit’s instructions.
Lean over a sink, tilt your head, and gently squirt or pour the solution into one nostril so it drains from the other. Breathe through your mouth.
Repeat on the other side, then gently blow your nose.
Rinse the device with safe water and let it air dry after each use.
Use once or twice a day while congested.

WHAT TO EXPECT: A clearer nose and easier breathing within minutes. Mild stinging at first is common, and it eases if the solution is the right strength.

WATCH OUT: Plain tap water can carry rare but dangerous organisms, so the water rule is not optional. Skip it if you have a blocked ear or recent nasal surgery. See a doctor if symptoms last more than 10 days or you have a high fever or facial pain.

As always, research thoroughly and consult a trusted professional before starting any new health protocol.

➡️  Washington reports first US bird flu death of 2026; health officials say risk to the public is low

- A person in Yakima County, Washington, who caught bird flu after being exposed to infected dairy cows has died following a severe illness, county health officials said Sunday.

- This is the first known person in the US to die from complications from avian influenza in 2026 and the third in the US to die from bird flu since February 2024, when the virus jumped into dairy cattle for the first time.

- ➡️  Washington reports first US bird flu death of 2026; he On October 31, the Yakima County Health District reported that a person who had come into contact with infected cattle was hospitalized with a severe case of bird flu. The person had underlying health conditions, but the county did not specify what they were. ➡️  On November 1, the county reported that the person had died. 

- Yakima County health officials said they are closely monitoring the contacts of the person who died to ensure that they didn’t pass the infection to anyone else.

- The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has recorded bird flu cases in more than 70 people in the US since 2024. Most of the people who’ve become ill have worked on farms with infected cattle or poultry. Health officials say that most cases have been mild and all have been so-called dead-end infections, in which a virus jumps from an animal to a person but doesn’t spread farther.

- No human-to-human transmission of bird flu has been documented in the US. Health officials say the risk to the public remains low.

- Three cases have been identified in people in the Yakima County Health District this year: a mild case identified last month, the person who died and a third case reported over the weekend.

- All three Washington cases have occurred since mid-October and resulted from exposure to infected cows. The third case, like the first case, has mild symptoms and has not been hospitalized, county health district officials said.

- State health officials said they have reported all three cases to the CDC. So far, the agency has not included them on its bird flu dashboard.

- Tracking bird flu cases in humans

- ➡️ Since October 8, 33 dairy herds infected with the H5N1 bird flu virus have been reported in Washington. The state is urging people who work at the dairies to wear personal protective equipment and report their symptoms if they feel ill.

- Dr. Dave Atteberry, the public health officer for the Yakima health district, said ➡️ the dairies with infected cows were found in early October through milk testing by the Washington State Department of Agriculture and the US Department of Agriculture.

- Public health ➡️ workers with the county then reached out to the affected farms and enrolled dairy workers in a text-based health screening tool that checks daily for symptoms including cough, fever or red eyes. If the workers report any, the health department follows up with additional questions, Atteberry told CNN last month.

“We’re throwing a large net so that we capture everybody that that potentially could be getting exposed, and then we’re able to focus our attention on those individuals that are exposed, and then we get them treated,” Atteberry said last month.

- ➡️ Not all states are approaching bird flu the same way. ProPublica recently reported that ⚠️ Utah’s Department of Agriculture and Food agreed to share information about bird flu outbreaks on farms ⚠️ as long as health officials didn’t take steps to track workers’ health.

- This patchwork state-by-state approach to monitoring bird flu infections in people is concerning, said Dr. Jennifer Nuzzo, who directs the Pandemic Center at Brown University’s School of Public Health.

- “I just think that our our picture of H5N1 is the murkiest it’s ever been,” Nuzzo said.

- ➡️ Nuzzo said this bird flu uptick at dairies in Washington, which has ➡️ coincided with the very early circulation of seasonal influenza on the Pacific Coast, sets the table for ➡️ the H5N1 virus to swap pieces of its genome with seasonal flu viruses. A big change like that ➡️ could potentially give the virus the tools it needs to better infect humans.

- “That is the bad scenario. So when you have an uptick in bird flu activity corresponding with human flu season, that just increases my worry even more that we could have a mix that we don’t want to have,” she said.

- On October 15, a dairy worker in the county tested positive for mild H5N1. It was the first human case reported in nearly a year.

- Atteberry said ➡️ farm workers who test positive are given antiviral medication with the goal of treating their symptoms as well as lowering their viral load to reduce the chance they could pass it to others.

- “Even though we haven’t seen that biologically be possible yet,” Atteberry said. “We’re doing it out of an abundance of caution.”

By Brenda Goodman

The correct answer is A. Generalized lymphadenopathy.
Explanation
Acute HIV Infection (Acute Retroviral Syndrome): Occurs 2 to 4 weeks after initial exposure and manifests as a flu-like or mononucleosis-like illness.
Generalized Lymphadenopathy: Prominent, non-tender, non-fluctuant lymph node enlargement (commonly involving cervical, axillary, and occipital nodes) is one of the most common physical examination findings during the acute phase. Other classic acute features include fever, sore throat, maculopapular rash, arthralgias, and myalgias.
Overview of Distractors
Ascites (B): Fluid accumulation in the peritoneal cavity, typically caused by cirrhosis/portal hypertension, heart failure, or severe hypoalbuminemia; it is not a feature of primary HIV infection.
Clubbing (C): Focal enlargement of the terminal phalanges, associated with chronic hypoxia or lung/cardiac diseases (e.g., bronchiectasis, lung cancer, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, cyanotic congenital heart disease).
Jaundice (D): Yellowish staining of the skin and sclera caused by hyperbilirubinemia, characteristic of acute/chronic hepatobiliary diseases or hemolytic anemias, but not a primary early sign of acute HIV.

No. What sounds 'fishy' is renouncing science without a suitable alternative! Are you familiar with just how the mRNA vaccines came to be?

Probably not, I take it...
See below, please.

Messenger RNA (mRNA) vaccine technology rests on decades of foundational research, culminating in the rapid development and widespread deployment of highly effective COVID-19 vaccines, followed by expansions into other indications.

The concept of using exogenous mRNA to direct protein production in cells emerged from basic molecular biology. Synthetic mRNA production methods were established in the mid-1980s, and early experiments in the late 1980s demonstrated that lipid-formulated mRNA could be taken up by cells to express proteins. By 1990, researchers showed protein expression after direct injection of mRNA into animal muscle. A decisive advance occurred in 2005, when Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman reported that incorporation of modified nucleosides (such as pseudouridine) markedly reduced inflammatory responses while enhancing protein translation. This modification, combined with advances in lipid nanoparticle (LNP) delivery systems, made clinical application feasible. Early clinical trials of LNP-mRNA vaccines against pathogens such as rabies and influenza, as well as exploratory cancer vaccine studies, confirmed immunogenicity in the 2010s. Companies including Moderna and BioNTech refined the platform during this period.

The COVID-19 pandemic provided the first large-scale validation. Following publication of the SARS-CoV-2 genome sequence in January 2020, Moderna and BioNTech (partnered with Pfizer) designed spike-protein-encoding mRNA candidates within days. Phase 3 trials completed later that year demonstrated efficacy of approximately 95 percent (Pfizer-BioNTech BNT162b2) and 94 percent (Moderna mRNA-1273) against symptomatic disease. Emergency use authorizations were granted in December 2020, with full approvals following in 2021. Billions of doses were subsequently administered worldwide. Real-world data confirmed substantial reductions in hospitalizations, severe disease, and deaths, particularly during earlier phases of the pandemic; U.S. estimates through early 2022 attributed millions of prevented deaths and hospitalizations to the vaccination program. Updated formulations have continued to provide measurable protection against severe outcomes amid evolving variants, although effectiveness against mild infection declines over time. In 2023, Karikó and Weissman received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for their nucleoside modification discoveries that enabled these vaccines.

The platform’s success has extended beyond COVID-19. Moderna’s mResvia (mRNA-1345), an RSV vaccine, received FDA authorization in May 2024 for older adults. In August 2026, the FDA approved Moderna’s mFLUSIVA (mRNA-1010), the first mRNA-based seasonal influenza vaccine, for adults aged 50+, based on Phase 3 data showing relative efficacy versus a standard-dose comparator. Personalized neoantigen mRNA cancer vaccines, notably Moderna and Merck’s intismeran autogene (mRNA-4157) combined with pembrolizumab, have advanced to Phase 3 and reported positive results in melanoma, delaying recurrence relative to immunotherapy alone. Additional candidates target other infectious diseases and oncology indications, leveraging the platform’s capacity for rapid sequence redesign.

In conclusion, the history of mRNA vaccines demonstrates a progression from decades of incremental scientific advances to a transformative public-health technology. The COVID-19 vaccines established the platform’s capacity for unprecedented speed, high efficacy against severe disease, and scalable global deployment. Subsequent regulatory approvals for RSV and flu  vaccines, together with promising clinical results in oncology, confirm the versatility of mRNA-LNP technology. These achievements have created a robust foundation for future applications against emerging threats
